items.title: Prompt Injection, Esq.: pwning AI agent guardrails with lawyerspeak
items.summary_1line: Prompt Injection, Esq.: pwning AI agent guardrails with lawyerspeak
items.editor_note: First practitioner report in the thread: a guardrail bypass built on legal-style phrasing.

editorial.tldr: This is a research cluster, not one event: late-October papers proposed model-level defenses (Heads of Security attention gates, SecPO adversarial training). Early-November papers widened the attack surface to agent memory, tool updates, task outcomes, and reasoning traces, and a Nov 8 paper argued for treating the model as an untrusted component.
editorial.whats_new: No new injection item since the Nov 11 "Prompt Injection, Esq." post on bypassing agent guardrails with legal-style phrasing; reclustering only added 14 adjacent long-horizon agent and evaluation papers.
editorial.why_it_matters: The thread keeps moving the defense out of the model: a guardrail that reads text can be argued with, so the control that holds is the one enforced in code around the tool call.
editorial.take_for_builders: Gate high-impact tool calls with deterministic policy and human approval instead of an LLM judge, then add legal-register, task-tampering, memory-poisoning, and tool-version-change cases to your red-team suite.

beats.headline: Attention gates and adversarial training target injection robustness
beats.summary: Heads of Security enforces instruction-data separation with learned per-head attention gates; SecPO proposes principled adversarial training.

beats.headline: Persistent memory and tool updates open gaps beyond single-session injection
beats.summary: MemHarmBench tests cross-session injection in memory-persistent agents; the Tool Update Gap paper shows frameworks may keep trusting tools after updates.

beats.headline: SPILLWAY separates target admission from sanitization
beats.summary: Argues against putting an LLM on the decision that lets an action through, since that decision can itself be manipulated.

beats.headline: Benchmarks add task tampering, thought injection, and weight-level injection
beats.summary: Two papers extend injection past instruction override, to task outcomes and the chain-of-thought stage; IWIBench is adjacent, covering one model editing another's weights rather than prompts.

beats.headline: Long-horizon agent and evaluation papers share the cluster, not the topic
beats.summary: Fourteen papers on long-horizon agents, memory, and benchmarks were grouped in by shared wording; none addresses prompt injection.

beats.headline: Paper frames injection as structural and treats the model as untrusted
beats.summary: Compares in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting) against deterministic policy enforcement, human approval, and taint tracking, validated on open-weights models.

beats.headline: Practitioner post claims guardrail bypass using lawyerspeak
beats.summary: The first non-paper item in the thread: a write-up on defeating agent guardrails with legal-style language.

open_questions: Do learned attention gates (Heads of Security) and SecPO training hold up against task-tampering and thought-injection attacks?
Do the memory and tool-update attack papers ship reproducible harnesses that independent teams can run?
Does SPILLWAY's admission/sanitization split keep its robustness in independent evaluation on real agent frameworks?
Which guardrail products does the lawyerspeak bypass work against, and do their vendors confirm or patch it?
Do deterministic policy enforcement and taint tracking hold on closed frontier models, beyond the open-weights models the paper validated on?
